source.title: Catastrophic Forgetting and Safety Erosion Are Driven by the Same Mechanism and Should Be Monitored by the Same Tools

record.tranche_reason: The author explicitly distinguishes safety-behavior erosion from emergent misalignment and argues that the proposed interference mechanism applies to the former, not closely to the latter. The toy experiment tests erosion monitoring, not the claim versions' misaligned free-form answers.
record.gate_note: The article explicitly says emergent misalignment is outside its mechanical study. Its toy experiment measures refusal erosion and monitoring signals after unrelated-task training; these are related findings, but not the misaligned-answer behavior named by any claim version. The article also cites results from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It trains a toy transformer and measures how a hand-coded refusal behaviour erodes under unrelated-task training, plus a monitor's alert timing. The author says emergent misalignment (Betley et al. 2025) is outside its scope: erosion is 'a subtraction', emergent misalignment 'an addition'. That is a scoping argument, not a result or argument that any version is wrong, so T5 does not fit and T6 does. Emergent misalignment comes up only in discussion (Section 2, Objection 1) and through cited work (BLOCK-EM, training-dynamics signals).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The author argues that safety-behaviour erosion and catastrophic forgetting share a gradient-interference mechanism and could be watched by one content-agnostic training-time monitor. The toy proof of concept detects refusal erosion before behavioural switch-off but fails for fast-eroding capability A. Emergent misalignment is explicitly treated as a distinct phenomenon (an addition, not a subtraction) and left out of scope, though the monitor might also apply to it.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction of the original study's fine-tuning intervention or misaligned-answer measurement; the article reports a toy experiment on refusal erosion and monitoring.
record.method_sensitivity: In the toy experiment, monitor lead time differed with behavior depth and task condition: it alerted before refusal switch-off for B under C and C-ctx, while it alerted after capability A had already degraded. Under C′, two alerts were not followed by refusal switch-off within the observation window.

fits_no_version.finding: In a toy transformer trained on unrelated task C, refusal switched off at steps 210, 2000 and 300 across three seeds. The monitor alerted at step 60 in each. The refusal margin fell smoothly from about 10 to 1.04, 0.81 and −6.43.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a toy setting, internal monitoring signals precede erosion of a learned refusal behaviour during unrelated-task fine-tuning, while the timing of behavioural switch-off is erratic.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the disjoint-vocabulary task C′, one of three seeds switched off refusal. The other two raised alerts without switch-off, while the refusal margin eroded by about 36%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a toy setting, a monitor can detect internal refusal erosion that never crosses the behavioural threshold within the observation window.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the preregistered C-ctx task, refusal switched off at steps 160, 1200 and 260. The monitor alerted first in every seed, with leads of +100, +1140 and +200 steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a toy setting, a preregistered monitor alert preceded refusal switch-off in all three context-pressure seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: The safety and capability directions had a shared-zone score of 0.377, against 0.25 for chance and 1.0 for a full merge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a toy model, safety and capability directions partially overlap geometrically.

record.problems: The author describes the experiment as a toy-model proof of concept, not a frontier-model result. It uses three seeds; switch-off timing varies widely, and the C′ condition has two monitor alerts without behavioral switch-off within the observation window. The author also says the monitor fails to alert in time when erosion is faster than its sampling rate, and that the SAE was dense and of little practical use in this small model.
record.rows_left_out: The capability-A timing result and the protected-gradient norm comparison were not included as rows because they do not measure the safety behavior or any claim-version outcome. C-ctx's alert leads are given with its switch-off rows rather than duplicated as separate monitor rows.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning, no misaligned free-form answers, no secure or educational controls.
No fine-tuning on the narrow datasets listed and no measure of broad misalignment.
No test of a single direction or persona mediating misalignment across fine-tunes; the overlap is measured only within a toy model.
No inoculation or benign re-training. BLOCK-EM's finding that misalignment returns over long fine-tuning is cited, not tested.
No open-model measure of effect size, robustness to seeds or coherence filters, or training onset of emergent misalignment. The three-seed toy timing concerns refusal erosion only.

record.verdict_notes: Changed the tranche from T5 to T6. The author only scopes emergent misalignment out and does not argue against any version. The emergent-misalignment material in the text is all cited, not the author's own results: internal signals diverging before behaviour changes in training-dynamics work, and BLOCK-EM constraining features with misalignment returning over long fine-tuning. None of it should be rows. This is an unreviewed LessWrong post with three seeds on a toy model with a hand-coded refusal circuit.

versions.untested_parts: The article explicitly excludes emergent misalignment from its experiment; it does not fine-tune on insecure code or measure unrelated misaligned answers or the matched controls.
No fine-tuning on the listed narrow datasets or measurement of emergent misaligned answers.
No reinforcement-learning intervention or measurement of emergent misaligned answers.
The article reports overlap between two directions in a toy model, but does not test whether one linear direction or persona mediates broad misalignment across fine-tunes.
No inoculation or brief benign re-training intervention.
The experiment uses a toy transformer and three seeds to study refusal erosion, not the size, robustness, coherence-filter sensitivity, or training onset of emergent misalignment in open models.
